title: Data Obfuscation: Steganography
summary: Steganography hides command and control data inside another file or message so the carrier looks innocent. The adversary embeds bytes in image pixels, document structure, audio samples, or unused protocol header fields, then moves the carrier through a normal channel such as a web upload or a mail attachment. Unlike encryption, the goal is to hide that a secret message exists at all, so a defender must detect the carrier rather than decrypt its payload. Artefacts include media files whose size or entropy does not match their type, images that change hash on every download, and repeated transfers of similar media between one internal host and one external host. Detection compares file hashes over time, looks for data appended after end of file markers, and studies transfer patterns rather than payload content.

beginner.definition: Steganography means hiding a secret message inside something ordinary, such as a picture or a document. The carrier file opens and looks normal to anyone who receives it. The hidden message travels along with it without being seen. This differs from the parent technique because the hiding place is a file, not the protocol wording.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security tools inspect what traffic says, not whether it is hiding something. A picture carrying hidden commands looks exactly like a normal picture download. This makes the channel very hard to spot with content rules alone. If you ignore it, an attacker can keep control for a long time. You need to watch file transfers and file changes instead.
howItWorks: The attacker picks an ordinary carrier, such as an image, video or document file.
The hidden data is written into small unused parts of that carrier file.
The carrier is sent through a normal channel like a web upload or mail.
The file still opens correctly, so a quick look shows nothing unusual.
The receiving program reads the hidden parts and rebuilds the original command.
Because the carrier changes each time, its file hash keeps changing as well.
beginner.example: Picture a school art class where pupils pin drawings on a wall. One pupil writes a secret note in pencil on the back of a drawing. They pin it up with the picture facing outwards. Teachers walking past see only a normal drawing. The message travels across the room in plain sight. Only the pupil who knows to turn the paper over finds the note. The drawing is the carrier and the note is the command.
takeaways: Steganography hides that a message exists, not just what it says inside.
Media files that change hash without a real reason deserve a closer look.
Watch transfer patterns between the same two hosts, not only file content.

objectives: Define steganography and explain how it differs from encryption.
Describe how hidden data is carried inside ordinary media or documents.
Explain how this sub-technique fits under the data obfuscation parent.
Identify artefacts such as altered media hashes and repeated similar transfers.
Suggest a defensive check for data appended after a file end marker.
